Indian prodigies create golden alchemy at Chemistry Olympiad Bag a rich haul of four golds and clinch joint top position worldwide against 93 competing nations By Sindhu Hariharan Updated - July 19, 2026 at 08:36 PM. | Chennai × Share WhatsApp X Facebook LinkedIn Messenger Reddit Mail https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/on-campus/india-continues-olympiad-streak-sweeps-all-gold-at-chemistry-olympiad/article71241078.ece Copy Winning Indian team at the International Chemistry Olympiad Indian STEM prodigies had a standout showing at the 58th International Chemistry Olympiad (IChO) held in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, bagging a historic all-gold medal haul and clinching the joint top position worldwide against 93 competing nations. This achievement was the latest in a streak of winning performances in Olympiads this year by Indian students, who picked up medals at the Biology and Physics Olympiads too. At the 37th International Biology Olympiad (IBO) 2026 held in Vilnius, Lithuania, from 12 to 19 July 2026, the Indian team of four students won one Gold and three silver medals. According to information from the Homi Bhabha Centre for Science Education, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (HBCSE TIFR), the four winners of the Chemistry Olympiad were Debadatta Priyadarshi (GOLD) from Bhubaneshwar, Odisha, Harshit Singla (GOLD) from Mandi Gobindgarh, Punjab, Kabeer Chillar (GOLD) from Delhi, and Sandeep Kuchi (GOLD) from Hyderabad. The Biology team comprised Bhavyaa Gunwal (GOLD) from Mahendragarh, Haryana, Soumil Maity (SILVER) from Howrah, West Bengal, Nishit Kalani (SILVER) from Pali, Rajasthan, and Anmol Kumar (SILVER) from Mansa, Punjab. India’s track record at the Chemistry Olympiad has been improving over the years, with the last ten appearances yielding a strike rate of 43 per cent gold and 53 per cent silver medals, HBCSE says. This was India’s 27th appearance at the IChO and its first-ever all-gold haul. Incidentally, this year’s IChO, held between July 10 and 19, had 363 students from 93 countries, making it the biggest IChO till date. In the Biology Olympiad, this was India’s 26th appearance. In the last ten years, the gold and silver strike rates have been 25 per cent and 68 per cent, respectively. Prof. Anwesh Mazumdar, the National Coordinator for Science Olympiads from HBCSE, TIFR, said that the challenge had both theory and experimental components, and the teams posted heartening performances in both. Each theory problem takes about one hour to solve, and it’s very rigorous, he added. Given that our schools and competitive exams are not tuned towards experiments, HBCSE’s preparation camps for the Olympiads focus deeply on the experimental side, which holds 40 per cent weightage, he said. As for how India can retain this talent, the professor noted that the solution lies in making India’s research institutions as robust as international ones. The students who win at these Olympiads are among the brightest in their countries and tend to get admissions in places such as MIT in the US, the professor said. Hence, to retain this talent, the solution lies in making India’s research institutions as robust as international ones, he added. Photograph: Berta Álvarez Acal Spain No eggs, no potatoes but ‘a lot of imagination’: how Spain cooked in war’s hunger years Book recreates recipes from period following end of Spanish civil war when people faced food shortages Stephen Burgen in Barcelona Wed 2 Sep 2026 05.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google F ew dishes are simpler to prepare than Spain’s signature dish of tortilla de patatas , which – aside from disputes about onions – requires nothing more than two basic ingredients and a pinch of salt. But where to begin if you have neither eggs nor potatoes? That is the question the chef and food writer Berta Álvarez Acal sets out to answer in Recetas de Guerra (Wartime Recipes), a compilation of recipes covering the years of hunger after the end of the Spanish civil war in 1939. In the case of the tortilla de patatas , the absent eggs and potatoes were substituted by moistened bread and onion to try to simulate the texture of an omelette. “There was a formula using water, bicarbonate of soda and a bit of oil which simulated an egg perfectly and the potatoes are substituted by bread to make a tortilla that really is delicious,” Álvarez said. View image in fullscreen ‘Fried calamari without the calamari’. Álvarez says the recipes were recreated and shared with friends and family. Photograph: Berta Álvarez Acal In the recipe for “fried squid without squid”, deep-fried onion rings masquerade as squid while the “wartime hake” is instead salt cod. As for the “wartime and postwar breakfast”, this consists of “coffee” made from a blend of barley, malt and chicory. “I got the idea for the book when I came across one of my great-aunt’s handwritten recipe books and I noticed that some of the recipes were marked ‘wartime’,” Álvarez said. “That led me to research recipes from other sources such as Ignacio Doménech, who wrote a book during the war about how to substitute ingredients and how to make the most of leftovers.” She added: “Doménech showed us hundreds of examples of how, with a lot of imagination, we could survive those terrible days of starvation.” Some of Doménech’s recipes, although born of privation, could well find themselves on the menu of an upmarket restaurant today, such as his rose petals with milk and honey. Álvarez did not just compile the recipes. “We recreated them and shared them with friends and family,” she said. “Some dishes, although they were prepared from scraps, surprised us as they were real gems, others were not so great.” The recipes in the book span the period from the founding of the second republic in 1931 to the phasing out of ration cards in 1952. In between, starvation stalked the land, especially in areas that supported the losing republican side in the civil war. According to Miguel Ángel del Arco Blanco, a historian at the University of Granada, between 1939 and 1942 about 200,000 people died of starvation in Spain. While people in the countryside could to some extent subsist on olives and whatever they could grow, Álvarez said “the hunger in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia was horrific”. “It may seem implausible,” she said. “But for far too long, food in the postwar period was far worse than during the war.” View image in fullscreen Children queuing for milk rations in Barcelona in 1937. Photograph: Daily Herald Archive/SSPL/Getty Images Produce previously fed to livestock such as beetroot and turnips found its way to the table while the shortage of protein meant pets, cats in particular, were at risk. “They were dangerous years for cats,” Álvarez said. “People used to put notices up in the hallway saying ‘please respect your neighbour’s cat’. But the cats lived on rats and were not good to eat.” Álvarez said that what she learned while researching the book was to make the most of every kind of produce, adding that the book was also a homage to the generation that lived through those grim years. “I think it’s important that everyone knows what our grandparents lived through because it marked them as a generation. They were incredibly strong.” Explore more on these topics Spain Europe Spanish food and drink Food news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Andrew Messenger/The Guardian Australia news Queensland homeless man shot with Taser after being given move-on order to make way for kite festival Exclusive: Advocate says homeless clearances should be halted after man is hospitalised during confrontation in Brisbane park Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Messenger Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A homeless man was shot with a Taser by police after attempting to take his own life during a tent city clearance, sparking calls for mental health considerations when dealing with move-on orders amid Queensland’s homelessness crisis. On 1 September, Moreton Bay city council rangers gave six homeless residents 24 hours to leave Pelican Park north of Brisbane, where Martin* had been living in a camper trailer, to make way for a kite festival this weekend. The 48-year-old said he was unable to comply with the move-on order because he had lost his driver licence due to a drink-driving conviction. “I was under the understanding that they were coming to basically take my shit,” he told the Guardian. “In times gone past, I’ve complied. “This time I can’t, and they told me that basically they’re going to impound everything.” The homeless man, who has prostate cancer, told the rangers he would rather die than lose his few possessions. “I said, ‘All right, well, if this is what you wish to do, then not a problem. Bring an ambulance and a body bag for me,’” Martin said. He then stabbed himself in the neck with a knife. Moments later he was shot with a Taser at least twice by police. He said he had not threatened anyone else before injuring himself. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email A spokesperson for the Queensland police said its officers had attempted to de-escalate the situation and disarm Martin, but were unsuccessful. “Immediate first aid was applied by officers to the man, who had sustained a serious self-inflicted injury,” they said. “The QPS remains committed to providing officers with mental health training, focusing on an informed awareness of different categories of mental illness and the application of appropriate strategies to safely respond to persons experiencing mental health distress.” Local homeless advocate Beau Haywood, founder of charity Nourish Street, said the incident showed what can go wrong if councils continued their enforcement-led approach to the state’s homelessness crisis. He said Moreton Bay should halt homeless clearances until they could show they were both safe and legal. Snapping point Martin, whose camp is part of a small tent city of about a dozen residents near the waterfront in Clontarf, is a former security guard who lost his job during the pandemic. He has lived homeless in the Moreton Bay area for more than three years, and is on the social housing waiting list. He’s not alone: Moreton Bay has the state’s longest social housing waiting list – 5,146 at last count in 2025 – and a major rough sleeping problem. Several tent cities in the area house hundreds of people. He said after it happened he woke up in an ambulance on the way to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s hospital. He had surgery to patch up his injuries, saw a mental health worker, and asked to be discharged so he could get back to his camper trailer to protect his belongings. The next day, the hospital booked him a taxi back to the park. He had not been seen by any health professional since his discharge, he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion A spokesperson for the Metro North health service said it was “unable to comment on the specific details of a patient’s situation to respect their privacy and confidentiality”. Moreton Bay was the first of many councils across the country to turn to enforcement as the solution to Australia’s worsening homelessness crisis . It made national headlines when it bulldozed a tent city in Lawnton, which the Queensland supreme court ruled a violation of the state’s Human Rights Act . Haywood said the council had halted clearances during and after the court case, but had recently restarted them after announcing it would designate a park for the homeless . State-owned land is Luke Quinn’s final refuge from council patrols — but soon even that meagre safety could disappear Read more Haywood said during clearances, homeless people like Martin could feel backed into a corner and it was inevitable that people would eventually snap. “I’ve seen it time and time again. Every move brings [someone’s mental health] down even further . And I think for that gentleman, he reached his point,” he said. “I think that if council were aware of his mental health and physical health, that maybe some more precautions should be taken. Some mental health treatment should have been offered at the time.” Haywood said the clearances should be halted until they could be done safely. Martin said he loved old movies, motorcycles and a long chat. He has refused treatment for his prostate cancer. He said before he died he wanted to see friends in Townsville and South Australia. He said one of his greatest joys was to cook for his homeless friends. Since the confrontation, Martin’s circumstances have not changed. He has not been offered housing, or an alternative place to stay. There are 44,294 Queenslanders on the social housing waiting list. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cvrlyl.text: Russia's leading independent newspaper closes after eviction Russia's leading independent newspaper closes after eviction Close Russia's leading independent newspaper has closed after being evicted from its offices and facing pressure from authorities. For 30 years, Novaya Gazeta published investigations into corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power in the country. On Monday, the team behind the newspaper had a final editorial meeting before packing up their belongings and leaving. The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia's media was highly diverse and that the newspaper's closure was part of "a standard rotational process". The BBC spoke to its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, about the closure. More on this story.
